name: Naftalan oil

card.summary: A heavy crude oil from Naftalan, Azerbaijan, used in spa bathing and ointments for skin conditions such as psoriasis and eczema, which proponents say improve skin appearance.
card.note: The oil is a mixture of aromatic hydrocarbons; refined versions are used in some clinics to reduce side effects.

quick.overview:
Naftalan oil is a dense, naphthenic crude oil from the town of Naftalan in Azerbaijan. It has been used for centuries in folk and spa medicine, and practitioners apply it for skin and joint conditions. Its looksmaxxing relevance is through skin: people with psoriasis, eczema or other chronic skin conditions use it hoping to clear visible plaques and rashes.

Soviet and later Croatian clinics published studies and follow-ups reporting therapeutic effects. Western audiences have been more sceptical, and media coverage has raised questions about its composition.
quick.how: In Naftalan spas, people are bathed in the oil, covered up to the neck, for sessions of roughly ten minutes. Purified oil is also combined with mineral water balneotherapy, and refined distillates are used in ointments and clinic treatments elsewhere, such as in Croatia.
quick.risks: Press coverage has described the crude oil as being largely naphthalene and polycyclic hydrocarbons, which are classed as carcinogenic with significant exposure. A Croatian review of the oil it analysed reported it was not carcinogenic, and clinics there use a refined distillate free of tar and aromatics to reduce side effects. People with skin conditions should consult a dermatologist.

lead: Naftalan oil (also spelled naphtalan) is a heavy crude oil from the town of Naftalan, Azerbaijan, used in alternative medicine and balneotherapy.[1] It is too heavy for normal export and is applied in spas for skin and joint conditions.[1]

People use it mainly for chronic skin conditions such as psoriasis, so visible skin appearance is the main link to looksmaxxing: clearer, less inflamed skin. Its use is part of health tourism in Azerbaijan.[1]
Its chemistry was studied from the 1870s and its therapeutic effects from the 1890s. Soviet researchers published many papers, which European audiences largely did not accept.[1]

chain: Claimed reduction in psoriasis or eczema flares
angle.text: Spa users bathe in the oil to treat chronic skin conditions, aiming for calmer, clearer skin. The effect is a claimed one, drawn from Soviet and Croatian clinical reports.

paras: Naftalan oil is a dense mixture of aromatics, naphthenes, asphaltenes and resins, with naphthenic acids up to about 3 percent by weight. Purified versions are mainly polycyclic hydrocarbons with naphthenic content up to 98.5 percent.[1]

The oil was used in antiquity and noted by Marco Polo, according to Wikipedia. Its chemistry was studied from the 1870s and therapeutic effects from the 1890s; output increased after around 1900 and oil was exported to Germany, but exports faded after the 1917 revolution. A health resort at the Azerbaijan Medical University was operating by 1936.[1]
The Naftalan Special Hospital for Medical Rehabilitation was founded in Ivanić Grad, Croatia, in 1989 and uses a refined distillate free of tar and aromatics.[1]

Spas in Naftalan use the oil for whole-body bathing, with the person covered up to the neck for about ten minutes. Purified oil is also paired with mineral waters. Early partially purified preparations were used as ointment for wounds and burns and compared favourably with Vaseline.[1]

In the 1970s, researchers at the University of Zagreb School of Medicine compared Azerbaijani oil with oil from Križ, Croatia; after laboratory tests and a trial with 770 patients in 1978 they concluded the oil they analysed was not carcinogenic. The Ivanić Grad hospital reported therapeutic effects in a 10-year follow-up of 10,000 patients.[1] Soviet researchers published many papers in the 20th century, but European audiences largely rejected the results.[1]
A 2006 New York Times article and a 2009 Independent article described the oil as largely naphthalene, which they stated was carcinogenic to humans.[1]

timeline.event: Health resort operating at Azerbaijan Medical University.[1]
Zagreb trial of 770 patients concludes the analysed oil was not carcinogenic.[1]
Naftalan Special Hospital founded in Ivanić Grad, Croatia.[1]
